e: Hansen (7-2, Barrett, J.): the unconstitutional applications must be realistic and substantial relative to the plainly legitimate sweep, and courts first adopt any fairly possible constitutional reading.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Hansen

q:
Which of the following are TRUE about Hansen?

I. Hansen defrauded noncitizens with a fake "adult adoption" path to citizenship.
II. The Court read "encourage or induce" as criminal-law terms of art covering intentional solicitation and facilitation.
III. The Court held the statute overbroad because it reached advocacy.
o: I and II only
I, II, and III
II and III only
I only
e: The Court held the statute not overbroad: construed as terms of art, it excluded advocacy.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Hansen

q: Why is overbreadth described as "unusual" and "strong medicine"?
o: It lets a litigant assert others' rights and voids laws with lawful uses.
It requires proof that the law has no valid application whatsoever.
It is available only against criminal statutes, never civil ones.
It authorizes courts to rewrite statutes to cure their defects.
e: A litigant whose own speech is unprotected may raise others' rights, and a law with lawful applications is invalidated. It is justified by chilling concerns.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Hansen

q: What is the constitutional-avoidance (Ashwander) principle as applied in Hansen?
o: Choose a fair constitutional reading, but never against clear text.
Avoid constitutional questions by dismissing the case on standing.
Always adopt the narrowest reading, even against the statute's text.
Invalidate any statute that has at least one unconstitutional reading.
e: Courts seek harmony, not "constitutional collision."
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Hansen

q: How does an ordinary facial challenge differ from an overbreadth challenge?
o: Ordinary: no valid applications (Salerno). Overbreadth: substantial protected speech.
Ordinary facial challenges require a smaller showing than overbreadth challenges do.
Only overbreadth challenges may be raised as a defense in criminal prosecutions.
They apply the same test, but overbreadth is limited to speech-restricting laws.
e: Overbreadth is the First Amendment's relaxed facial-challenge rule: substantial protected speech relative to the plainly legitimate sweep.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Hansen

q: Why did Stevens strike down its statute while Hansen upheld its statute?
o: Construction: Stevens's text reached many real protected uses; Hansen's terms of art didn't.
Stevens involved criminal penalties, while Hansen involved only civil immigration penalties.
Hansen's own speech was protected advocacy, while Stevens's own videos were unprotected.
Stevens applied rational-basis review, while Hansen applied strict scrutiny to the statute.
e: Stevens read § 48 by ordinary meaning, so hunting videos were realistic, numerous protected applications. Hansen read "encourage or induce" as solicitation and facilitation, leaving only fanciful concerns.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Stevens vs. Hansen

q: A new federal law bans selling videos of actual dogfights that were illegal where filmed. What is the government's strongest defense?
o: It is narrow and fits speech integral to crime.
Depictions of animal cruelty became an unprotected category after Stevens.
The law is content-neutral, so only intermediate scrutiny applies to it.
Videos of real events aren't speech under the First Amendment at all.
e: The law answers the question Stevens left open, and like Ferber, the market drives the underlying crime. Alternatively, it may survive strict scrutiny by targeting the commercial incentive.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Dogfight-video stretch

q: In the dogfight-video problem, which is a strong argument AGAINST the law?
o: Prosecuting the fights themselves is less restrictive.
Videos of dogfights are not speech at all.
The law is content-neutral and therefore invalid.
Stevens abolished speech integral to crime.
e: Challengers also argue that Ferber rests on harm to children, "illegal" where is unclear, and the ban sweeps in journalism and exposés.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Dogfight-video stretch

q: What is the outline's likely answer on the narrow dogfight-video ban?
o: Defensible if narrowly drafted and tied to the crime
Clearly unconstitutional under Stevens's reasoning
Clearly valid as a new animal-cruelty category
Valid only if it exempts all journalism about dogfights
e: Beyond the casebook, Congress's 2010 crush-video law was limited to obscene videos, tying it to an existing category.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Dogfight-video stretch

q: A city ordinance says: "Speeches about sports teams are prohibited in the public square." What type of rule is this, and what scrutiny applies?
o: Content-based; strict scrutiny
Viewpoint-based; intermediate scrutiny
Content-neutral; intermediate scrutiny
Content-neutral; rational basis
e: A subject-matter restriction is content-based and gets strict scrutiny.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Types of rules

q: A state allows vanity license plates but rejects "FCANCER" while accepting other expressive plates. What type of rule is this?
o: Viewpoint-based, the worst form; strict scrutiny
Content-neutral time, place, and manner rule; intermediate scrutiny
Government speech that is exempt from First Amendment review
Obscenity regulation reviewed under the three-part Miller test
e: The outline lists the FCANCER plate as viewpoint-based, the worst form. A cancer survivor won in 2024.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Types of rules

q: An ordinance says: "No blasting speeches through amplifiers between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m." What type of rule is this?
o: Content-neutral; intermediate scrutiny
Content-based; strict scrutiny
Viewpoint-based; strict scrutiny
A prior restraint; heavy presumption against it
e: It regulates time and manner without regard to message (Ch. 9).
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Types of rules

q: A state bans publications that advocate legalizing marijuana while allowing publications that oppose legalization. What is the proper classification?
o: Viewpoint-based; strict scrutiny
Content-neutral; intermediate scrutiny
Unprotected incitement to crime
Speech integral to criminal conduct
e: Favoring one side of a debate is viewpoint discrimination. Advocacy of legalization is protected abstract advocacy.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Types of rules

q: What do all the cases in Chapter 4 have in common regarding unprotected-category arguments?
o: Every case rejected the unprotected-category argument.
Every case held the speech was in an unprotected category.
They all applied rational-basis review to the challenged law.
They all expanded an existing category to reach new speech.
e: Know why each argument failed (see the synthesis table). The categories are defined very narrowly by Justices across the spectrum.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Chapter 4 overview

q: What rule did Terminiello v. City of Chicago (1949) announce?
o: Speech can't be punished for stirring anger or unrest.
Hate speech to a packed auditorium is incitement.
Breach-of-the-peace laws are invalid on their face.
Speech that risks clashes with protesters is fighting words.
e: Terminiello (5-4, Douglas, J.): speech must pose a clear and present danger of a serious evil far above public inconvenience or annoyance.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Terminiello

q: Why was Terminiello's conviction reversed even though the facts sounded like incitement?
o: The jury instruction swept in protected speech.
The priest's speech was protected religious exercise.
The protesters outside caused the real disturbance.
The city lacked statutory authority to prosecute him.
e: Breach of the peace was defined to include speech that "stirs the public to anger, invites dispute, brings about a condition of unrest." The reading tip is to start with the law as construed.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Terminiello

q: What did the Terminiello dissent (Vinson, Frankfurter, Jackson, Burton) argue?
o: That counsel failed to object to the instruction
That the priest's speech was fighting words
That clear and present danger should be abandoned
That hate speech is an unprotected category
e: The dissent rested on the lack of an objection, not on a different First Amendment rule.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Terminiello

q: According to Terminiello, why may speech serve its purpose best when it induces unrest?
o: The alternative is standardized ideas.
Unrest proves that the speech is true.
Unrest makes the speech newsworthy.
Unrest lets the government regulate it.
e: Speech may best serve its high purpose when it stirs people to anger. Collin later relied on this passage.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Terminiello

q: Under Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), advocacy of force or law violation may be punished only if it is:
o: Directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it
Likely to cause serious harm at some point in the foreseeable future
Advocacy of the moral propriety or necessity of violence against the state
Delivered at an assembly organized for the purpose of advocating violence
e: Four elements: intent (directed to), imminence, lawless action, and likelihood.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Brandenburg

q:
Which of the following are TRUE about Brandenburg?

I. It was a 9-0 per curiam decision that overruled Whitney v. California.
II. Only Klan members and journalists were present at the rally.
III. Ohio's criminal syndicalism law required intent, imminence, and likelihood.
IV. The KKK leader warned of possible "revengeance" and announced a march on Congress.
o: I, II, and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
II and III only
I and III only
e: Ohio's law punished mere advocacy with no intent, imminence, or likelihood requirement. That's why it fell.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Brandenburg

q: Brandenburg distinguished abstract teaching of the necessity of force from what?
o: "Preparing a group for violent action and steeling it to such action"
Advocacy delivered in a traditional public forum such as a park
Speech by organized groups rather than by individual speakers
Speech that criticizes the national government during wartime
e: Abstract teaching is protected; preparing and steeling a group is not.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Brandenburg

q: What did the Black and Douglas concurrences in Brandenburg argue?
o: The clear-and-present-danger test should be expressly rejected.
Clear and present danger should be kept, with an imminence element added.
The Klan leader's conviction should have been upheld on the facts.
The case should have been decided under the Religion Clauses instead.
e: That test had been used to affirm WWI dissidents' convictions (Abrams, Schaefer, Pierce). Douglas quoted Holmes in Gitlow: "Every idea is an incitement."
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Brandenburg

q: Match the era to its standard. Which is correct?
o: 1919-27: bad tendency used against dissidents; 1969-now: intent, imminence, likelihood
1919-27: intent, imminence, likelihood; 1969-now: bad tendency used against dissidents
1949-51 (Terminiello, Dennis): bad tendency; 1969-now: clear and present danger
1919-27: fighting words doctrine; 1949-51: true threats doctrine
e: 1919-27 (Abrams, Schaefer, Pierce, Whitney) used clear and present danger or bad tendency. The middle era (Terminiello, Dennis) used clear and present danger of serious evil.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Incitement eras

q: A philosophy professor lectures to a class that violent revolution is sometimes morally necessary to overthrow unjust governments. She is prosecuted for advocating violence. Result?
o: Protected as abstract teaching about the morality of force.
Unprotected, because students are impressionable.
Unprotected under the bad-tendency test.
Protected only if she disclaims violence.
e: Brandenburg protects abstract teaching of the moral propriety of force absent intent, imminence, and likelihood.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Brandenburg

q: At a rally outside a jail, a speaker points at the doors and shouts to an angry, armed crowd: "Break in now and drag him out!" The crowd surges forward. Result?
o: Unprotected incitement to imminent lawless action.
Protected, because it criticizes the justice system and its jailers.
Protected, because each member of the crowd made his own choice.
Protected unless and until the crowd actually breaks into the jail.
e: Intent, imminence, lawless action, and likelihood are all present.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Brandenburg

q: At a rally, a speaker says: "We'll take the streets again next month if the council doesn't listen." A state convicts him of incitement. Which Brandenburg element is weakest for the state?
o: Imminence of the lawless action
That the speech is advocacy
That the speaker is identifiable
That the rally was public
e: A threat of action "next month" lacks imminence. (Beyond casebook, Hess v. Indiana made a similar point.)
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Brandenburg

q: What are "fighting words" under Chaplinsky?
o: Personal insults likely to provoke an immediate attack
Any speech that openly advocates fighting or violence
Speech offending a group based on race or religion
Profanity spoken aloud in a public place
e: Insults so offensive they're likely to provoke the listener to attack the speaker immediately. The Court hasn't upheld a restriction on this theory since 1942.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Fighting words

q: Why was Cohen's "Fuck the Draft" jacket NOT fighting words?
o: No direct personal insult and no realistic prospect of violence
Profanity can never qualify as fighting words under Chaplinsky
The jacket was worn inside a courthouse rather than on a street
Cohen removed the jacket and apologized when asked by officers
e: Fighting words require a direct personal insult likely to provoke immediate violence. No one present could reasonably see one.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Fighting words

q: What does the "no heckler's veto" principle (Cox v. Louisiana; Edwards v. South Carolina) hold?
o: Speakers can't be convicted over a hostile crowd police could control.
Hecklers may be arrested whenever they disrupt a lawful speaker.
Speakers must stop talking once the crowd becomes visibly hostile.
Government may ban speech that is likely to attract hostile crowds.
e: Peaceful civil rights protesters can't be convicted because a hostile crowd might become violent when police can control it.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Hostile audience

q: A peaceful group protests at a statehouse. Counter-protesters gather and threaten to attack. Police, who have enough officers on hand to maintain order, instead arrest the original protesters for breach of the peace. Result?
o: The convictions are unconstitutional as a heckler's veto.
The convictions are valid because the protesters provoked the hostility.
The convictions are valid under Chaplinsky's fighting-words doctrine.
The convictions are valid because the protest was at a government building.
e: This is a heckler's veto when police could control the crowd (Edwards; Cox).
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Hostile audience

q: Why did Collin v. Smith fall outside both Brandenburg and Chaplinsky?
o: The village conceded it expected no violence.
The marchers had obtained a permit.
A swastika isn't a symbol.
The march was on private property.
e: Without expected violence, neither incitement nor fighting words applies. Hate speech is generally protected.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Hate speech

q: During an argument on a sidewalk, a man steps inches from another man's face and hurls a string of personal slurs at him, clearly trying to goad him into swinging. Which category is the closest fit, and what's the catch?
o: Fighting words, but the doctrine hasn't been used since 1942.
Incitement under Brandenburg, because the words provoke violence by the listener.
A true threat under Counterman, because the speaker was at least reckless.
Obscenity under Miller, because slurs are patently offensive to the listener.
e: A direct, face-to-face personal insult likely to provoke immediate attack is the core of Chaplinsky, but the Court hasn't upheld a restriction on that theory since 1942.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Fighting words

q: What rule did R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul (1992) announce?
o: A whole unprotected category may be banned, but not a topic or viewpoint subset.
Cross burning is protected speech in all circumstances, even as a threat.
Fighting words are no longer recognized as an unprotected category.
Hate-speech ordinances are valid so long as they are limited to fighting words.
e: R.A.V. (9-0 on the judgment, Scalia, J.): unprotected categories aren't "invisible to the Constitution."
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — R.A.V.

q:
Which of the following are TRUE about R.A.V.?

I. The ordinance was construed to reach only fighting words.
II. It covered symbols arousing anger based on race, color, creed, religion, or gender.
III. It was underinclusive because it didn't reach fighting words based on political affiliation, union membership, or sexual orientation.
IV. The Court held the ordinance valid as applied to cross burning.
o: I, II, and III only
I, II, III, and IV
II and IV only
I and III only
e: The ordinance was held facially unconstitutional.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — R.A.V.

q: A state makes it a crime to publish libel, but only libel that criticizes government officials. Libel against private persons remains subject only to civil suit. Under R.A.V.:
o: Unconstitutional subset discrimination.
Valid, because libel is unprotected speech.
Valid, because protecting officials is compelling.
Valid under intermediate scrutiny.
e: Government may ban libel, but not only libel critical of the government. This is R.A.V.'s own example.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — R.A.V.

q: A city bans ALL fighting words, regardless of topic, in public places. Under R.A.V., which is correct?
o: R.A.V. permits banning the whole category, though Chaplinsky's narrow definition still applies.
R.A.V. forbids any regulation of fighting words, whether of the whole category or a subset.
The ban must satisfy strict scrutiny because banning fighting words is content-based.
The ban is viewpoint-based, because it silences only speakers who choose to insult.
e: R.A.V. objects to topic or viewpoint subsets, not to regulating the whole category for the reason it is proscribable.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — R.A.V.

q: What did the 1993 Harvard note (by coauthor Klein) argue about Chaplinsky?
o: It should be overruled, not expanded.
It should be expanded to reach all hate speech.
It should be merged into the incitement test.
It should apply only in public schools.
e: It rewards the undesirable response of fighting (unlike fleeing a false "Fire!") and gives police discretion to punish minorities and critics.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — R.A.V.

q: Under the prior-restraint checklist, what defines a prior restraint and what follows?
o: Stopping speech before it occurs; a heavy presumption of invalidity
Punishing speech after it occurs; strict scrutiny of the penalty
Any content-neutral rule; intermediate scrutiny of its fit
Any rule aimed at the press; rational-basis review
e: Injunctions and licensing are prior restraints. The government bears a heavy burden, and the only recognized exception is Near's wartime dictum, never actually applied.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Prior restraint

q: What happened in Near v. Minnesota (1931)?
o: The Court reversed an injunction against articles alleging police corruption.
The Court upheld an injunction against a paper publishing troop movements.
The Court held newspapers liable for defaming public officials.
The Court upheld a state licensing scheme for local newspapers.
e: The Framers especially opposed prior restraints. Dictum: in wartime, the government might prevent publication of troop numbers and locations or transport sailing dates.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Near v. Minnesota

q: A county judge enjoins a local blog from publishing further posts accusing the sheriff of taking bribes. Result?
o: An invalid prior restraint under Near.
Valid, because the posts may be defamatory.
Valid if the sheriff shows likely harm.
Valid, because blogs aren't the press.
e: Near struck down an injunction against publishing accusations of official corruption. Any remedy for defamation comes after publication.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Near v. Minnesota

q: During an ongoing war, a newspaper plans to publish the sailing dates and routes of troop transports. The government seeks an injunction. Which is the best answer?
o: This fits Near's dictum, though the Court has never applied it.
The injunction is clearly invalid, because prior restraints are never permitted.
The injunction is valid as incitement under Brandenburg.
The injunction is valid under R.A.V.'s whole-category rule.
e: Near's dictum names troop numbers, locations, and transport sailing dates.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Near v. Minnesota

q: Which is TRUE about New York Times Co. v. United States (1971)?
o: A 6-3 per curiam denied injunctions against publishing a classified study.
It is the defamation case that set the actual-malice standard for officials.
It upheld a 15-day injunction as a permissible wartime prior restraint.
It held that the press has no right to publish leaked classified documents.
e: A general claim of national-security harm didn't meet the heavy burden. Don't confuse it with NYT v. Sullivan. Publication was restrained for 15 days before the ruling.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Pentagon Papers

q: What was Justice Black's position (with Douglas) in the Pentagon Papers case?
o: Every moment of restraint was a flagrant violation.
A real likelihood of grave danger should be enough.
The decision was too rushed to be made responsibly.
Restraints should cover only tactical military plans.
e: Black added that the press serves the governed, not the governors, and "security" is a vague generality. The dissent (Burger, Harlan, Blackmun) complained of haste.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Pentagon Papers

q: In the Pentagon Papers briefs, what did the ACLU argue?
o: Restraints should be limited to military operations, weapons designs, and codes.
A "real likelihood" of grave danger to national security should suffice.
The President is best placed to judge national-security harm from publication.
Prior restraints are always permissible while the nation is at war.
e: The ACLU said restraints should never be allowed for information bearing on public policy decisions. The government argued the "real likelihood" and presidential-judgment positions.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Pentagon Papers

q:
Which is TRUE about the aftermath of the Pentagon Papers case?

I. The Court has never upheld such a restraint.
II. Marchetti and Snepp rested on CIA secrecy agreements.
III. The Progressive H-bomb article injunction was affirmed by the Supreme Court.
o: I and II only
I, II, and III
II and III only
I only
e: The Progressive was enjoined in the lower court, but the case was abandoned before appeal.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Pentagon Papers

q: Why did the unprotected-category argument fail in each case? Which pairing is correct?
o: Terminiello: reached speech that merely angered; R.A.V.: banned a topic subset
Terminiello: police could control the crowd; R.A.V.: no direct personal insult
Brandenburg: village conceded no violence; Cohen: presumption not overcome
Collin: punished mere advocacy; Near: banned only a topic-based subset
e: Brandenburg: mere advocacy. Cohen: no personal insult. Cox/Edwards: police could control. Collin: no expected violence. Near/Pentagon Papers: presumption not overcome.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Chapter 4 synthesis

q: An activist livestreams outside a courthouse: "we need to shut this courthouse down today." Viewers push barricades. The activist adds: "I'm not telling anyone to hurt anybody. But history remembers people who act." Ten minutes later a group breaks through. What is the government's BEST evidence of intent?
o: Urging escalation after seeing the pushing
Criticizing the government and its courts
Reaching a large online audience
Naming the courthouse as the target
e: The post-pushing statement is the government's best evidence. The outline calls the case close, turning on intent.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Courthouse livestream

q: In the courthouse livestream problem, which is the activist's strongest argument?
o: "Shut it down" is common protest rhetoric, and violence was disclaimed.
Livestreamed video isn't speech protected by the First Amendment.
Courthouse steps are nonpublic forums where no speech is protected.
Incitement requires the speaker to personally commit the violence.
e: The activist also stresses core criticism of government, a largely online audience, and heckler's-veto concerns. The outline calls it close; a properly instructed jury could convict. Beyond the casebook, Hess and Claiborne Hardware support the activist.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Courthouse livestream

q: Which pairing correctly states the mens rea each case requires?
o: Brandenburg: intent; Counterman: recklessness; Williams: belief and intent
Brandenburg: recklessness; Counterman: intent; Williams: negligence
Brandenburg: negligence; Counterman: objective test; Williams: knowledge
Brandenburg: intent; Counterman: objective test; Williams: recklessness
e: Mens rea gives honest speakers "breathing room" at the cost of letting some unprotected speech go unpunished.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Mens rea theme

q: What rule did Counterman v. Colorado (2023) announce?
o: True threats require proof the speaker was at least reckless.
True threats are judged by a purely objective reasonable-recipient test.
The prosecution must prove the speaker specifically intended to threaten.
Messages sent online can never qualify as true threats of violence.
e: Counterman (7-2 on the judgment, Kagan, J.): the threat is judged by how a reasonable recipient would understand it, plus a subjective recklessness floor.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Counterman

q:
Which of the following are TRUE about the facts of Counterman?

I. He sent hundreds of Facebook messages over two years to a musician he'd never met.
II. He created new accounts when blocked.
III. He was convicted under a stalking law applying a purely objective test.
IV. The Court affirmed the conviction.
o: I, II, and III only
I, II, III, and IV
I and II only
III and IV only
e: The Court vacated and remanded.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Counterman

q: What does "true" in "true threat" exclude?
o: Jests and hyperbole
Threats made online
Threats not carried out
Threats to public figures
e: For example: "I'll kill you if you leave dirty dishes in the sink."
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Counterman

q: Why did Counterman choose recklessness rather than purpose or knowledge?
o: It balances chilling against the harm threats cause.
It is easier for prosecutors to prove than negligence.
Purpose would make threats identical to fighting words.
It is the same standard used in defamation cases.
e: Reckless speakers consciously accept a substantial risk of serious harm. A subjective element prevents self-censorship by speakers unsure of the line.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Counterman

q: Match each Counterman opinion to its standard.
o: Majority: recklessness; Sotomayor concurrence: intent; Barrett dissent: objective only
Majority: intent; Sotomayor concurrence: recklessness; Barrett dissent: negligence
Majority: objective only; Sotomayor concurrence: intent; Barrett dissent: recklessness
Majority: recklessness; Sotomayor concurrence: objective only; Barrett dissent: intent
e: The majority was Kagan, Roberts, Alito, Kavanaugh, and Jackson. Gorsuch joined Sotomayor in part; Thomas joined Barrett.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Counterman

q: Why did Justice Sotomayor's concurrence in Counterman favor an intent standard?
o: Online speech lacks context, and incitement requires intent.
Intent is required for every crime under the Due Process Clause.
The victim's fear should be irrelevant to whether speech is a threat.
Recklessness is unconstitutionally vague as applied to online speech.
e: She also noted that juries' norms and stereotypes vary. The dissent would let legislatures calibrate using an objective test.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Counterman

q: A man repeatedly posts about his ex-partner: "Someone should put a bullet in her. Watch your back." He knows many readers would see this as threatening but posts anyway because he doesn't care. Under Counterman:
o: Recklessness is satisfied because he consciously disregarded the risk.
He can't be convicted unless he intended to threaten her.
He can't be convicted because the posts were made online.
He can't be convicted because he said "someone," not "I."
e: Consciously disregarding a substantial and unjustifiable risk that the words would be seen as threats is recklessness.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Counterman

q: A socially isolated man sends messages that a reasonable recipient would find threatening, but the evidence shows he genuinely had no awareness they could be seen that way. He is convicted under a purely objective test. Under Counterman:
o: The conviction can't stand, because an objective test alone is not enough.
The conviction stands because a reasonable recipient would feel threatened.
The conviction stands under the dissent's approach, which is controlling here.
The conviction stands because the messages were sent repeatedly over time.
e: The First Amendment requires at least recklessness; an objective test alone is insufficient. This is Counterman itself.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Counterman

q:
Which of these is speech integral to criminal conduct (unprotected)?

I. "Your money or your life"
II. "I'll sell you heroin"
III. "I'll tell you when the coast is clear"
IV. "Cocaine should be legal"
o: I, II, and III only
I, II, III, and IV
II and IV only
I only
e: Abstract advocacy of illegality ("cocaine should be legal") stays protected.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Speech integral to crime

q: Which are the categories of speech integral to crime described in the outline?
o: Speech that is the crime; offers or solicitations; aiding or concealing a crime
Any speech about crime; fictional depictions of crime; news reports on crime
Advocacy of illegality; harsh criticism of police; true threats of violence
Written offers to sell contraband, but not spoken offers or requests
e: Examples: "Your money or your life," "I'll sell you heroin," and a conspirator's lookout. Hard cases include general-audience how-to material.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Speech integral to crime

q: What rule did United States v. Williams (2008) announce?
o: Offers and requests for contraband are unprotected.
Pandering laws are overbroad because they reach advocacy.
Any statute that produces close cases is void for vagueness.
Offers are protected unless the material actually exists.
e: Williams (7-2, Scalia, J.) relied on Giboney and Pittsburgh Press. A law is vague only if it fails to give fair notice or invites seriously discriminatory enforcement.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Williams

q: How did Williams construe "promotes"?
o: Recommending a particular item with intent to transfer it
Any speech encouraging people to possess such material
Including abstract advocacy that the material be legalized
Limited to paid commercial advertisements for the material
e: "Promotes" doesn't reach "child pornography should be legal" or even "I encourage you to obtain it," distinguishing abstract advocacy (Brandenburg; Claiborne Hardware).
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Williams

q: What does Williams say about vagueness?
o: It is a Due Process doctrine about indeterminate terms.
It is a First Amendment doctrine about overbroad laws.
Any statute that produces close cases is vague.
Belief and intent are inherently vague elements.
e: Vagueness concerns indeterminacy about what fact must be proved ("annoying," "indecent"), not difficulty proving it. Belief and intent are true-or-false facts, and proof problems go to reasonable doubt.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Williams

q: Who dissented in Williams, and on what basis?
o: Souter and Ginsburg, on statute-specific grounds
Scalia and Thomas, arguing the material is protected
Kennedy alone, arguing the statute was too vague
Breyer and Kagan, arguing for intermediate scrutiny
e: The dissent didn't dispute that speech integral to crime is unprotected.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Williams

q: Which statement correctly contrasts vagueness and overbreadth?
o: Vagueness is Due Process and about one's own speech; overbreadth is First Amendment and about third parties.
Vagueness comes from the First Amendment; overbreadth comes from the Due Process Clause.
Vagueness lets litigants assert third parties' rights; overbreadth covers only their own.
They serve different goals: vagueness prevents chilling, overbreadth prevents unfair notice.
e: Vagueness: the law is unclear (Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project). Overbreadth: the law reaches too much protected speech (Stevens, Hansen). Both aim to prevent chilling.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Vagueness vs. overbreadth

q: A city ordinance makes it a crime to "engage in annoying conduct on public sidewalks." A defendant challenges it. Which doctrine is the best fit?
o: Void for vagueness
Prior restraint
Fighting words
Speech integral to crime
e: "Annoying" is indeterminate about what fact must be proved. Williams used it as its example of a vague term.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Vagueness

q: What rule did Rice v. Paladin Enterprises (4th Cir. 1997) announce?
o: Publishing that intentionally aids a crime, and is used as intended, is unprotected.
All instructional manuals describing how to commit crimes are unprotected speech.
Publishers are immune from aiding-and-abetting liability for what readers do.
News reporting about crime can support civil liability if a reader copies it.
e: Paladin published Hit Man, which Perry used to murder three people. The First Amendment didn't bar the families' aiding-and-abetting suit.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Rice v. Paladin

q:
Which of the following are TRUE about Rice v. Paladin?

I. Paladin stipulated that it intended to assist murderers.
II. Copycat cases, where readers misuse novels and films, differ because publishers don't intend to assist crime.
III. News reporting is never a basis for liability.
IV. The holding means all how-to manuals are unprotected.
o: I, II, and III only
I, II, III, and IV
II and IV only
I and III only
e: The stipulations, detailed instructions, exhortation to murder, and lack of any legitimate purpose made the case unique.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Rice v. Paladin

q: According to the outline, why is Paladin unlikely to be repeated often?
o: Intent evidence rarely exists without stipulations.
The Supreme Court later reversed the decision.
Publishers now print disclaimers in such books.
Aiding-and-abetting liability has been abolished.
e: The stipulations were what made the case possible.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Rice v. Paladin

q: A reader copies a murder method described in a bestselling crime novel. The victim's family sues the publisher, citing Paladin. Result?
o: The publisher is likely protected, because it didn't intend to assist crime.
The publisher is liable because the method was used exactly as described.
The publisher is liable because crime novels are a form of how-to material.
The publisher is liable unless it proves it lacked knowledge of the risk.
e: Copycat cases differ: novels are protected because their publishers don't intend to assist crime. Paladin rested on stipulated intent.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Rice v. Paladin

q: A publisher releases a detailed bomb-making manual with no stipulations about intent. What should the government have to prove to impose liability, per the outline?
o: Specific intent, extrinsic evidence, actual use, and narrow construction
Only that the manual contains dangerous technical information
That a reasonable reader would find the manual threatening
That the manual lacks serious value under the Miller test
e: Intent as in Brandenburg (not Counterman's recklessness), evidence beyond the text, actual use in a crime, and narrow construction (Hansen). Beyond the casebook, 18 U.S.C. § 842(p) takes this approach.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Bomb-manual stretch

q: Which argument AGAINST liability in the bomb-manual problem is strongest?
o: It has legitimate audiences, and there's no extrinsic intent evidence.
Publishers are categorically exempt from aiding-and-abetting liability.
Building a bomb is legal in most states, so no crime is being aided.
The manual is a work of fiction and so receives full protection.
e: Engineers, researchers, journalists, and novelists are legitimate audiences; general publication isn't a one-to-one offer like Williams; and Stevens bars creating categories by balancing.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Bomb-manual stretch

q: What did Garcia v. Character Technologies (M.D. Fla. 2025) hold at the preliminary stage?
o: The court wasn't ready to call chatbot output speech and denied dismissal.
Chatbot output is fully protected speech, so the suit was dismissed.
AI companies are immune from tort suits under the First Amendment.
Chatbot output is unprotected as speech integral to a crime.
e: A distributor may assert users' right to receive speech, but output counts only if expressive. This was the first wrongful-death suit against an AI chatbot company, involving a 14-year-old's suicide.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Garcia v. Character Technologies

q: On which opinion did Garcia rely to question whether LLM output is speech?
o: Barrett's Moody v. NetChoice concurrence
Kagan's Counterman majority opinion
Scalia's Brown opinion on video games
Kennedy's Free Speech Coalition opinion
e: An algorithm carrying out a human's expressive choice may be speech, but when owners "hand the reins" to an LLM, it's unclear anyone made an expressive choice.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Garcia v. Character Technologies

q:
Why did the AI company in Garcia rely on its USERS' rights rather than claim the output as its own expression?

I. Claiming the output would mean owning its words and the liability for them.
II. It would admit deliberate design, like Paladin's stipulations, helping prove intent.
III. It would reinforce the product-design framing.
o: I, II, and III
I and II only
III only
II and III only
e: Beyond the casebook, it would also undercut Section 230 immunity for third-party content.
topic: Ch. 5 · True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime — Garcia v. Character Technologies

q: What unites the "immoral speech" categories in Chapter 6?
o: Suppression for reasons of morality
All are unprotected categories
All involve depictions of violence
All involve commercial speech
e: The categories are obscenity, sexually explicit speech, child pornography, profanity, and violent imagery.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Immoral speech overview

q: What does "indecent" mean in the outline?
o: Immoral but not obscene
A synonym for obscene
Unprotected for minors
Profanity on the radio
e: Indecent speech is generally protected, with Pacifica as the narrow exception.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Immoral speech overview

q: What are the two overarching questions in the immoral-speech checklist?
o: Who is protected, adults or kids? Is the harm from the content or indirect?
Is the speech political or commercial? Was it distributed for profit?
Was the speaker reckless? Was the listener part of a captive audience?
Is the medium broadcast or print? Does the speech contain profanity?
e: The second question asks whether the harm comes from the content itself or indirectly, such as exploitation of real children.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Immoral speech checklist

q:
Which of these governing principles are TRUE?

I. Government almost never can restrict immoral speech to protect adults from its content, with obscenity as the exception.
II. Government can sometimes protect kids, but it can't block adult access, and kids have their own First Amendment rights.
III. Local governments may zone adult businesses to reduce secondary effects.
IV. Virtual child pornography may be banned to dry up the market for abuse.
o: I, II, and III only
I, II, III, and IV
I and II only
II, III, and IV only
e: Ferber covers material made with actual children, not virtual images or adult look-alikes (Free Speech Coalition).
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Governing principles

q: What rule did Bolger v. Youngs Drug Products (1983) announce?
o: Kids may be shielded only if adults keep access.
Contraceptive advertising is unprotected speech.
Unsolicited mail may be banned to protect children.
Mail recipients are a captive audience.
e: Bolger (9-0 on the bottom line, Marshall, J.): government can't shield adults from immoral content (except obscenity) and "may not reduce the adult population to reading only what is fit for children."
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Bolger

q:
Which of the following are TRUE about Bolger?

I. Shielding adults from offense "carries little weight."
II. "The short, though regular, journey from mail box to trash can is an acceptable burden."
III. Helping parents control children's exposure was "undoubtedly substantial," but the ban failed.
IV. Recipients of mail are a captive audience.
o: I, II, and III only
I, II, III, and IV
I and IV only
II and III only
e: Recipients aren't a captive audience. Parents already control their mail, and the ban purged material suitable for adults.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Bolger

q: Bolger quoted Butler v. Michigan for which idea?
o: Such a ban would "burn the house to roast the pig."
Obscenity is not within the area of protected speech.
Broadcasting is uniquely pervasive in American life.
Offensive speech may be kept out of the private home.
e: Mailbox discourse can't be limited to "that which would be suitable for a sandbox."
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Bolger

q: How did Bolger distinguish Pacifica?
o: As narrow, because broadcasting is uniquely pervasive and accessible to kids
As overruled by later cases involving cable and satellite television
As an obscenity case that turned on the Miller test's three prongs
As a case that applied only to criminal prosecutions of broadcasters
e: Mail doesn't share broadcasting's special characteristics.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Bolger

q: A state bans mailing unsolicited catalogs for adult sexual-wellness products to homes, citing the need to protect children who might open the mail. The catalogs aren't obscene. Result?
o: Likely unconstitutional, because it purges material suitable for adults.
Valid, because protecting children is a compelling interest.
Valid, because the home gets special protection under Pacifica.
Valid, because the products are widely viewed as immoral.
e: The ban purges material suitable for adults, parents already control their mail, and recipients can throw it away.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Bolger

q: Which is TRUE about Cohen v. California (1971)?
o: Harlan wrote for a 5-4 Court reversing the conviction.
It upheld the conviction because children were present.
It held that profanity is obscene in public places.
It held courthouses are places where profanity can be banned.
e: Cohen wore "Fuck the Draft" in a Los Angeles courthouse corridor and got 30 days for offensive conduct. Unwilling viewers could avert their eyes.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Cohen v. California

q: A protester wears a T-shirt with a profane anti-war slogan in a public library lobby where children are present. He is convicted of offensive conduct. Under Cohen:
o: The conviction likely violates the First Amendment.
The conviction is valid because children were present.
The conviction is valid under Pacifica's nuisance rationale.
The conviction is valid because libraries are quiet zones.
e: Unwilling viewers can avert their eyes, and the presence of unwilling viewers doesn't automatically justify suppression.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Cohen v. California

q: What did FCC v. Pacifica Foundation (1978) hold?
o: Indecent broadcasts may be regulated, on a narrow nuisance rationale.
Indecent speech is unprotected in every medium, including print.
The FCC may criminally prosecute broadcasters for any expletive.
George Carlin's monologue was obscene under the Miller test.
e: Broadcasting is uniquely accessible to children, and context is all-important. Pacifica was 5-4 on the bottom line, with a plurality by Justice Stevens.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Pacifica

q:
Which of the following are TRUE about the facts of Pacifica?

I. The "Filthy Words" monologue aired at 2 p.m.
II. A father driving with his young son complained.
III. The FCC imposed heavy criminal fines.
IV. The FCC issued a declaratory order finding the broadcast indecent.
o: I, II, and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
II and III only
I and III only
e: The FCC issued a declaratory order without formal sanctions.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Pacifica

q:
Why is broadcasting "special" under Pacifica?

I. Children have access to radios, often unsupervised.
II. Radios are in the home, where privacy gets extra deference.
III. Unconsenting adults may tune in without warning.
IV. Spectrum is scarce and licensed in the public interest.
o: I, II, III, and IV
I and II only
III and IV only
I, II, and III only
e: All four reasons appear in the outline.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Pacifica

q: Which quotation reflects Pacifica's nuisance rationale?
o: "a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard"
"burn the house to roast the pig"
"I know it when I see it"
"Every idea is an incitement"
e: Time of day, program content, and medium all matter.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Pacifica

q: How did Pacifica contrast Cohen?
o: The broadcast "could have enlarged a child's vocabulary in an instant."
Cohen involved obscenity, while the Carlin broadcast did not.
Cohen involved a captive audience, while radio listeners were not.
Cohen was itself a broadcast case decided under the same rule.
e: Cohen's written message might have been incomprehensible to a first grader. The medium's accessibility to children was the difference.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Pacifica

q:
Which questions did Pacifica expressly leave undecided?

I. Two-way radio
II. An occasional expletive
III. Criminal prosecution
IV. A 2 p.m. broadcast of a repetitive profane monologue
o: I, II, and III only
I, II, III, and IV
IV only
II and IV only
e: IV is the case Pacifica decided. Pacifica returns in Ch. 9 (time, place, and manner).
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Pacifica

q: A radio station airs the same Carlin monologue at 2 a.m., preceded by a warning. Why might the analysis differ from Pacifica?
o: Context is all-important, and time of day matters.
It wouldn't differ; indecent broadcasts are always unprotected.
The warning would make the broadcast obscene under Miller.
Late-night radio isn't speech under the First Amendment.
e: Pacifica stressed time, content, and medium. Children are less likely to be listening at 2 a.m., and the warning reduces surprise for adults.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Pacifica

q: What is the key takeaway from Cohen and Pacifica together?
o: Profanity is protected; Pacifica is the narrow exception.
Profanity is unprotected whenever children may be present.
Profanity is protected only in written, not spoken, form.
Profanity is protected for adults but never for minors.
e: Calling speech "indecent" or "profane" generally doesn't mean it can be restricted (Cohen; the FCANCER plate).
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Cohen and Pacifica

q: Under Miller v. California (1973), which set of requirements must ALL be met for speech to be obscene?
o: Prurient appeal under community standards; patently offensive sexual conduct defined by state law; no serious value, taken as a whole
Sexually explicit content; offensiveness to a reasonable person; a complete absence of any value whatsoever to anyone
Depiction of nudity; commercial sale or distribution; a realistic likelihood that minors could access the work
A judge's own sense that "I know it when I see it"; patent offensiveness; and prurient appeal to the judge
e: All three prongs must be met, and Miller is still good law. Value means serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Miller test

q: What does "prurient interest" mean?
o: A shameful or morbid interest in sex
Any interest in sex at all
Interest in violent imagery
Interest in material for minors
e: "A shameful or morbid interest in nudity, sex, or excretion," not a normal interest in sex (Brockett v. Spokane Arcades, 1985).
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Miller test

q: Which Miller prong "matters most," according to the outline, and why?
o: Prong (c), serious value
Prong (a), community standards
Prong (b), state-law definitions
None; all count equally
e: Prong (c) protects works that, as a whole, have value, even if isolated scenes might seem obscene.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Miller test

q: Before Miller, what did Justice Stewart famously say about obscenity, and in which case?
o: "I know it when I see it," in Jacobellis (1964)
"Every idea is an incitement," in Gitlow
"A pig in the parlor," in Pacifica
"Unanimity of the graveyard," in Barnette
e: The Court's "movie days" gave lower courts little guidance.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Miller test

q: A prize-winning literary novel contains three sexually explicit scenes that, read in isolation, a jury might find patently offensive. The state prosecutes the bookseller for obscenity. Most likely result?
o: Not obscene, because the work as a whole has serious literary value.
Obscene, because any patently offensive scene suffices.
Obscene, because local community standards control.
Not obscene, because novels are always protected.
e: The work is judged as a whole, and serious literary value defeats an obscenity finding.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Miller test

q: Why wasn't the Hudnut ordinance saved as an obscenity regulation?
o: It didn't track Miller's elements.
It tracked Miller but was vague.
It regulated only violent images.
It applied only to broadcasting.
e: No prurient-interest requirement, no offensiveness, no community standards, no work-as-a-whole inquiry, and value was irrelevant. Its drafters saw those omissions as virtues; the court saw viewpoint discrimination.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Hudnut revisited

q: What did Renton v. Playtime Theatres (1986) hold?
o: Adult-business zoning gets intermediate scrutiny as a secondary-effects rule.
Adult theaters show obscene material and may therefore be banned outright.
All zoning laws that affect speech must satisfy strict scrutiny.
Secondary effects justify regulating any speech that attracts crime.
e: Such zoning targets crime and property values, not the message, even though it's partly content-based. The Court has refused to extend it beyond adult entertainment.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Renton

q: A city restricts bookstores selling extremist political literature to an industrial zone, citing studies that such stores attract crime. It invokes Renton. Most likely result?
o: Renton doesn't help; strict scrutiny applies.
Valid under Renton's intermediate scrutiny.
Valid, because crime is a secondary effect.
Valid, because the literature is incitement.
e: The Court has refused to extend secondary-effects doctrine beyond adult entertainment establishments.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Renton

q: What did New York v. Ferber (1982) hold?
o: Child pornography made with real children is unprotected, even if not obscene.
Child pornography is unprotected only if it is also obscene under Miller.
All sexual depictions of minors, including virtual images, are unprotected.
Possession of child pornography is protected when it occurs in the home.
e: Distribution is intrinsically related to the abuse of the children used to make it. Unanimous on the bottom line (White, J.), upholding a law covering children under 16.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Ferber

q:
Which of the following are reasons given in Ferber?

I. Preventing child sexual exploitation is an objective of "surpassing importance."
II. The materials are a permanent record, and circulation worsens the harm.
III. Drying up the market may be the only practical enforcement method.
IV. The material's value is "exceedingly modest, if not de minimis."
o: I, II, III, and IV
I and II only
I, III, and IV only
II and IV only
e: Production is clandestine, but marketing requires a visible apparatus.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Ferber

q: What does the casebook note say Ferber's rationale resembles?
o: Secondary effects
Incitement
Fighting words
Obscenity
e: The harm is indirect (abuse of real children in production), not caused by the message.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Ferber

q: What did Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition (2002) hold?
o: Ferber doesn't reach images made without real children.
Virtual child pornography is unprotected under Ferber.
The CPPA was valid because it protected children.
Explicit images of young-looking adults are obscene.
e: The CPPA's ban on images that "appear to" depict minors (computer-generated images or adult look-alikes) went beyond Ferber.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Free Speech Coalition (2002)

q:
Which of the following reasons did Free Speech Coalition give?

I. Teen sexuality and abuse are enduring themes in art; Juliet is 13.
II. "Appear to be under 18" exceeds many states' ages for marriage and consent.
III. Artistic merit doesn't depend on the presence of a single explicit scene.
IV. Ferber itself relied on virtual images as a permissible alternative.
o: I, II, III, and IV
I and II only
III and IV only
I, II, and IV only
e: All four appear in the outline.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Free Speech Coalition (2002)

q: Which is TRUE about the lineup in Free Speech Coalition (2002)?
o: 6-3 by Kennedy; Rehnquist and Scalia dissented.
9-0 by Scalia, with no separate writings.
5-4 by Rehnquist, with Kennedy dissenting.
6-3 by Thomas, with O'Connor dissenting.
e: Thomas concurred in the judgment; O'Connor concurred in part and dissented in part.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Free Speech Coalition (2002)

q: A state bans all computer-generated sexually explicit images of fictional minors, created without any real child, regardless of value. Under the outline's cases:
o: The ban likely fails, since no real child is involved.
The ban is valid under Ferber.
The ban is valid because the images appear to depict minors.
The ban is valid under Renton's secondary-effects doctrine.
e: Ferber's rationale depends on real children. Such images can be reached only if obscene under Miller or offered as depicting real children (Williams).
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Free Speech Coalition (2002)

q: A seller advertises images he claims depict real children. The images are actually computer-generated. He is prosecuted under a pandering law like the one in Williams. Result?
o: He can be punished for offering material represented as depicting real children.
He can't be punished, because virtual images are protected under Free Speech Coalition.
He can't be punished unless the images are also obscene under Miller.
He can be punished only if a real child was harmed in making the images.
e: Offers of material represented or believed to involve real children are speech integral to crime, even if the belief is mistaken. Technology makes it nearly impossible to prove which images involve real children.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Williams revisited

q: What did Ashcroft v. ACLU (2004) ("Ashcroft II") hold?
o: COPA likely failed strict scrutiny because filters were a less restrictive alternative.
COPA was valid under intermediate scrutiny because its burden on adults was incidental.
Online speech receives less First Amendment protection than printed speech.
Age verification by credit card is always a sufficient defense to such laws.
e: Ashcroft II (5-4, Kennedy, J.): the government must prove less restrictive alternatives wouldn't be as effective.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Ashcroft II

q:
Why were filters considered a less restrictive and possibly more effective alternative in Ashcroft II?

I. Filters restrict at the receiving end, not the source, and adults needn't identify themselves.
II. No speech is criminalized, so chilling is diminished.
III. Filters block foreign sites, can't be evaded by minors with credit cards, and cover email.
IV. Filters are perfect.
o: I, II, and III only
I, II, III, and IV
I and II only
III and IV only
e: Filters are imperfect, but the government offered no specific evidence that COPA would work better.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Ashcroft II

q: What did Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton (2025) hold?
o: Age verification for material obscene as to minors gets intermediate scrutiny.
Age-verification laws get strict scrutiny, and Texas's law fails it.
Age-verification laws get only rational-basis review.
Adults have no right to access sexual content online.
e: Paxton (6-3, Thomas, J.) upheld Texas H.B. 1181 because the burden on adults is incidental.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Paxton

q: Which two traditional state powers did Paxton rely on?
o: Banning obscenity, and shielding kids from what is obscene as to them
Zoning adult businesses, and licensing broadcasters in the public interest
Punishing fighting words, and regulating misleading commercial speech
Banning all sexually explicit material, and requiring filtering software
e: The second power is Ginsberg v. New York (1968), which adjusted the Miller test for minors.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Paxton

q: How did Paxton distinguish Reno v. ACLU (1997)?
o: The CDA in Reno effectively banned adult speech.
Reno involved broadcast rather than the internet.
Reno was expressly overruled by Ashcroft II.
Reno involved obscenity rather than indecency.
e: Reno applied strict scrutiny because its age-verification defense was illusory given the technology. The internet has changed dramatically since Reno and Ashcroft II.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Paxton

q: Why did Paxton reject rational-basis review?
o: Adults have a real, if incidentally burdened, right.
Rational basis never applies to any speech regulation.
Texas itself asked the Court to apply strict scrutiny.
Rational basis applies only to federal statutes.
e: Rational basis applies only when no fundamental rights are implicated. Intermediate scrutiny is "deferential but not toothless."
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Paxton

q:
Which points did Paxton make in applying intermediate scrutiny?

I. The interest in shielding children from sexual content is "important, even compelling."
II. Age checks using ID or transactional data are used for gambling, alcohol, tobacco, and car rentals.
III. Less restrictive alternatives like filters defeat the law.
IV. Stigma has never exempted the industry from regulation.
o: I, II, and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
II and III only
I and III only
e: Under intermediate scrutiny, less restrictive alternatives don't defeat a legitimate legislative choice.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Paxton

q: Did Paxton effectively overrule Ashcroft II? What is the key point?
o: Filters won in 2004 but lost in 2025 because the standard of review dropped.
Yes; Paxton expressly overruled Ashcroft II and Reno v. ACLU together.
No; Paxton applied strict scrutiny, just as Ashcroft II had done.
No; filtering software was never considered as an alternative in Ashcroft II.
e: The Court framed the earlier cases as involving effective bans on adult access. The change in scrutiny level changes how less restrictive alternatives count.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Paxton vs. Ashcroft II

q: What did Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association (2011) hold?
o: There is no unprotected category for violence, even for minors.
Violent video games are obscene as to minors under Ginsberg.
Video games aren't speech because players interact with them.
States may ban violent games for minors under intermediate scrutiny.
e: Brown (7-2, Scalia, J.): California's ban on selling violent video games to minors failed strict scrutiny. Alito and Roberts concurred; Thomas and Breyer dissented.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Brown v. EMA

q: Why did Brown distinguish Ginsberg v. New York?
o: Ginsberg adjusted an existing category for minors.
Ginsberg involved broadcasting, not retail sales.
Ginsberg had been overruled by Miller.
Ginsberg involved violence, not sex.
e: California sought a wholly new category for children only. Obscenity covers only depictions of sexual conduct, not violence.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Brown v. EMA

q:
Which of the following are TRUE about Brown?

I. Video games are speech because they communicate through characters, dialogue, plot, music, and interaction.
II. Grimm's fairy tales, the Odyssey, and Lord of the Flies show there's no tradition of restricting violence for kids.
III. Interactivity makes video games different in kind from literature.
IV. There is no "free-floating power to restrict the ideas to which children may be exposed."
o: I, II, and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
II and III only
I and III only
e: Interactivity differs in degree, not kind (choose-your-own-adventure books). Judge Posner: all literature is interactive.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Brown v. EMA

q:
Why did California's law fail strict scrutiny in Brown?

I. The research showed correlation, not causation, with minuscule effects.
II. It was wildly underinclusive (Bugs Bunny cartoons and E-rated games have similar effects).
III. The industry's rating system already helps parents, so filling a "modest gap" isn't compelling.
o: I, II, and III
I and II only
III only
I and III only
e: Underinclusiveness alone was enough to defeat the law.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Brown v. EMA

q: A state requires websites hosting graphic violent content to verify users' ages to keep minors out, citing Paxton. Best analysis?
o: Brown controls; strict scrutiny likely applies.
The law is valid under Paxton's intermediate scrutiny.
Violence is obscene for minors under Ginsberg.
The law is valid because adults keep their access.
e: Paxton's framework rests on speech obscene as to minors. Brown refused to create a violence category even for children.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Brown v. EMA

q: Which pairing from the Chapter 6 synthesis table is correct?
o: Paxton: intermediate, upheld; Ashcroft II: strict, struck
Paxton: strict, struck; Ashcroft II: intermediate, upheld
Brown: intermediate, upheld; Renton: strict, struck
Ferber: protected, struck; Free Speech Coalition: unprotected, upheld
e: Brown: strict, struck. Renton: intermediate, upheld. Ferber: unprotected, upheld. Free Speech Coalition: protected, struck.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Chapter 6 synthesis

q: Which case in the synthesis table involved protecting ADULTS AND KIDS, with the speech held protected and the ban struck?
o: Bolger (contraceptive ads)
Pacifica (indecent broadcast)
Ferber (child pornography)
Renton (adult business zoning)
e: Bolger protected both, and the interests were insufficient.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Chapter 6 synthesis

q: A 15-year-old consensually sends her own explicit image to a 15-year-old partner. Does Ferber's rationale fit?
o: Poorly, because the image is self-made and shared with a peer.
Perfectly; any explicit image of a minor is Ferber material.
Not at all, because teens have full rights to such images.
Only if the image is also obscene under Miller.
e: Ferber's market-and-exploitation rationale fits poorly for a self-made image shared consensually with a peer.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Teen sexting stretch

q: In the teen-sexting problem, the 15-year-old partner forwards the image to classmates without consent. Which Ferber harm now fits well?
o: The permanent record
The commercial market
The de minimis value
The prurient appeal
e: Nonconsensual redistribution fits Ferber's second harm: a permanent record whose circulation worsens the injury.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Teen sexting stretch

q: What "sensible rule" does the outline suggest for teen sexting?
o: One turning on exploitation
Prosecute all teen sexting
Never regulate teen sexting
Look only at the partner's age
e: An adult partner or nonconsensual redistribution looks like Ferber; a consensual exchange between peers doesn't. The outline also asks whether the partner's age (15, 17, 18, 25) matters.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral Speech — Teen sexting stretch
